title: Energy-transition legitimacy is being renegotiated through affordability, geopolitical dependence and confidence in the grid
source_unit: Ipsos, Energy Transition Barometer 2026 / Global Advisor study
geography: 31 countries; global, regional and country comparisons

energy_cost_worry.unit: percent worried about rising energy costs

spending_cutbacks.unit: percent who have cut other spending to cover rising energy costs

foreign_energy_dependency_baseline.unit: percent worried their country relies too heavily on foreign energy sources before the Iran conflict

energy_independence_preference.unit: percent saying their country should prioritize energy independence even at higher costs

observations.method: Ipsos Global Advisor survey on energy affordability, dependence, independence and household trade-offs, with baseline fieldwork in January and February 2026.
observations.uncertainty: The estimates are public attitudes and reported household behavior; they do not measure actual bills, energy use, policy effectiveness or whether cost worry produces durable political change.
observations.subgroup: Adults under 75 across 31 countries, with regional and country variation.
observations.counterinterpretation: Respondents may support energy independence in principle while opposing specific infrastructure, taxes or local projects needed to deliver it.

observations.period: February–May 2026; follow-up fieldwork after the Iran conflict

denominator.unit: Ipsos Global Advisor follow-up respondents across the 31-country study; follow-up analytic denominator not separately headlined

foreign_energy_dependency_followup.unit: percent concerned their country relies too much on foreign energy sources

dependency_anxiety_change.unit: percentage-point increase between February and May 2026

largest_country_increases.value: Australia +16 points, Singapore +13, India +13 and Great Britain +12

observations.method: Ipsos before-and-after public-attitude comparison using baseline and follow-up fieldwork around the Iran conflict.
observations.uncertainty: The comparison captures a temporal shift around a geopolitical shock but is not a randomized causal design; other news, prices, seasonal conditions and domestic politics may contribute.
observations.subgroup: Adults across 31 countries, with especially large reported shifts in Australia, Singapore, India and Great Britain.
observations.counterinterpretation: The shift may reflect general conflict salience or media attention rather than a durable reassessment of energy policy and dependence.

observations.period: 2026; electricity reliability and AI data-centre capacity

denominator.unit: adults under age 75 across 31 countries in the Global Advisor study

future_electricity_confidence.unit: percent confident their region can meet future electricity demand

ai_data_centre_grid_readiness.unit: percent believing local grids are ready for the energy needs of AI data centres

blackout_worry.unit: percent worried about unplanned outages in the coming year

observations.method: Cross-national survey of perceived electricity-system capacity, reliability and AI data-centre readiness.
observations.uncertainty: Perceptions of grid readiness are not engineering assessments or forecasts of actual outages; the question may be interpreted differently across countries and levels of public knowledge.
observations.subgroup: Adults under 75 across 31 countries; Ipsos notes advanced economies are notably more skeptical about AI data-centre readiness than emerging markets.
observations.counterinterpretation: Low confidence may represent precaution or unfamiliarity with data-centre load growth rather than a measured local capacity shortfall.

denominator.unit: adults under age 75 across 31 countries in the Global Advisor study

renewables_storage_support.unit: percent supporting investment in renewable energy and storage

low_price_priority.unit: percent wanting governments to prioritize low energy prices even if emissions rise

nuclear_opposition.unit: percent opposed to increased nuclear development

observations.method: Ipsos comparison of public support for transition investment, price prioritization and energy technologies across 31 countries.
observations.uncertainty: Support for broad transition categories does not predict support for specific facilities, siting decisions, rate structures or permitting trade-offs.
observations.subgroup: Adults under 75 across 31 countries, with country and regional variation.
observations.counterinterpretation: The apparent contradiction between transition support and low-price priority may reflect a demand for clean energy that is also reliable and affordable, not rejection of climate action.

related_sources.claim: Official Ipsos report PDF with fieldwork, energy-cost, independence, reliability and transition-preference findings.
Official Ipsos energy topic page contextualizing the 2026 Energy Transition Barometer.

boundary: This record adds a geopolitical-energy legitimacy mechanism: a conflict shock makes foreign dependence more salient, while affordability pressure, household cutbacks, grid reliability and AI load concerns condition support for the energy transition. It is a cross-national public-opinion study with a before-and-after comparison, not a causal conflict experiment, engineering reliability assessment, household billing panel or proof that broad transition support translates into local project consent.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official Ipsos Energy Transition Barometer page and downloadable People and Climate Change 2026 PDF were retrieved and reviewed for sample, energy-cost worry, spending cutbacks, foreign dependence, conflict-period change, grid readiness, AI data-centre reliability, transition support, solar and nuclear preferences; the PDF was hashed.
